summary: Proverbs 22 (29 verses) continues the story of wisdom. Starting with 'A good name is more desirable than great riches, and loving favor is better than silver and gold.', it moves through themes of wisdom, fear of LORD and calls readers toward practical life.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows wisdom lived out in royal court wisdom. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: A good name is more desirable than great riches, and loving favor is better than silver and gold.
Folly is bound up in the heart of a child; the rod of discipline drives it far from him.
Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will serve kings. He won’t serve obscure men.

questions.question: What is happening in Proverbs 22?
questions.answer: In 29 verses, this chapter proverbs 22 (29 verses) continues the story of wisdom. starting with 'a good name is more desirable than great riches, and loving favor is better than silver and gold.', it moves through themes of wisdom, fear of lord and calls readers toward practical life. The setting is royal court wisdom, written to young, community. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Proverbs and why 22 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally solomon and others, addressed to young, community around ~950-700 bc compiled. This chapter fits the book's purpose as proverbs — its themes of wisdom, fear of LORD build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'grace' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Undeserved favor/gift. In this chapter, it appears in context of wisdom. For a first-time reader: think of it as undeserved favor/gift, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through wisdom and fear of LORD, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: What is the main takeaway for a first-time reader?
questions.answer: Read once for story (who, what, where), once for repeated words (what themes repeat?), and once asking: what does this ask me to trust or do? This chapter's outline 1-9, 10-18, 19-29 helps you track movement.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
